title: Autoregressive Language Modeling (Decoder-Only)
oneLineScope: Decoder-only, left-to-right language modeling: the GPT lineage and its causal factorization.
prose:
A language model assigns a probability to a sequence of words (or, in modern practice, of subword tokens — pieces of text produced by a learned vocabulary; see the tokenization node). The oldest and most natural way to factor that probability is the chain rule of probability, applied left to right: write the joint distribution over a sequence of length \(n\) as a product of conditionals,

\[ p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} p(x_t \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{t-1}). \]

You already know this factorization from n-gram models and from HMMs: the Markov assumption was just a device to make each factor tractable. The question has always been how to parameterize the conditional \(p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\) richly enough to capture long-range dependencies without exploding in parameters. The transformer's self-attention mechanism gives a principled answer: let each position attend directly to every preceding position in one parallel operation, with no Markov truncation at all.

Stripping the encoder and cross-attention

Recall the full transformer from Vaswani et al. (2017): an encoder that reads a complete source sequence with bidirectional full self-attention, and a decoder that generates the target one token at a time, attending to the encoder's output via a cross-attention sublayer. For a generative language model — not translation, not summarization, just modeling text — there is no separate source sequence. The encoder and the cross-attention layer become vestigial. Drop both. What remains is a stack of \(L\) decoder blocks, each containing only two sublayers: causal (masked) self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network (FFN), both wrapped in residual connections and layer normalization. This stripped decoder is the decoder-only transformer; it is the architectural kernel of the GPT lineage.

The residual stream is \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\), one row per token position, flowing up through \(L\) identical blocks. At the top, a linear projection maps \(X\) to logits in \(\mathbb{R}^{n \times V}\) (where \(V\) is the vocabulary size), and a row-wise softmax turns each row into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The model's prediction at position \(t\) is \(p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})\); the right-shifted target alignment — position \(t\) predicts token \(t+1\) — is what makes every position in the sequence contribute a loss signal in a single forward pass.

The causal mask is the mechanism

The left-to-right constraint is enforced entirely by the attention mask introduced in the scaled dot-product attention node. Before the row-wise softmax, every above-diagonal entry of the \(n \times n\) score matrix is set to \(-\infty\), sending its attention weight to exactly zero. Position \(t\) therefore receives contributions only from positions \(1, \ldots, t\) in the value-weighted mixture. The attention mechanism is otherwise unchanged: every position still computes its query and key scores against all \(n\) positions in one matrix multiply, so the computation is fully parallel across the sequence even though the information flow is strictly causal. This is what separates the decoder-only architecture from the old recurrent models: the LSTM could only process one step at a time because its hidden state literally depended on the previous one; the causal transformer processes all positions simultaneously and enforces the ordering constraint algebraically, not sequentially.

Training objective

The model is trained to minimize the mean cross-entropy over all positions in all training sequences:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1}). \]

Here \(\theta\) denotes all learnable parameters (the projection matrices \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\) in each attention layer, the FFN weights, the embedding matrix, and the output projection). The loss is computed over the gold tokens (the true next tokens from the training data) — this training regime goes by the name teacher forcing: at training time the model always receives the correct prefix \(x_{<t}\), never its own predictions, which sidesteps the exposure-bias issue at the cost of a train/test gap. Note that \(p_\theta(x_t \ | \ x_{<t})\) is a distribution over all \(V\) vocabulary items; the loss is the negative log probability assigned to the actual next token. In information-theoretic terms this is the perplexity objective: minimizing cross-entropy is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood of the training data, which drives the per-token perplexity toward the entropy of the true distribution.

Generation: autoregressive decoding

At inference time the teacher-forcing shortcut is gone. The model starts from a prompt (a prefix of tokens) and extends it one token at a time: run a forward pass over the current sequence, extract the distribution at the last position, sample or select a token, append it, repeat. This is autoregressive decoding — each new token feeds back as part of the context for the next step, hence the name. Two selection rules dominate in practice: greedy decoding always picks the argmax, \(\hat{x}_t = \arg\max_v p_\theta(v \mid x_{<t})\), which is deterministic but can loop or degenerate on long outputs; sampling draws from the distribution (sometimes with a temperature parameter that sharpens or flattens it), which introduces stochasticity and tends to produce more varied text. Nucleus (top-p) sampling, which restricts the draw to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold \(p\), is the most common practical variant, though those refinements are downstream of the core architecture.

GPT-1 and GPT-2: the recipe in practice

Radford et al. (2018) — GPT-1 — demonstrated that a decoder-only transformer pre-trained on large unlabeled text could be fine-tuned on downstream tasks with minimal task-specific architecture changes. GPT-1 used \(L = 12\) decoder blocks, \(d_{\text{model}} = 768\), \(h = 12\) attention heads, and approximately 117 million parameters; training data was BooksCorpus (~800M words). The two-stage procedure — generative pre-training on language modeling, then supervised fine-tuning on labeled data — was not new in spirit (it echoes transfer learning in vision and the pre-training/fine-tuning split in ELMo and ULMFiT), but demonstrating it cleanly at this scale with a transformer was the contribution.

GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) scaled the same recipe: 48 layers, \(d_{\text{model}} = 1600\), up to 1.5 billion parameters for the largest variant, trained on WebText (~40GB of web text filtered through Reddit upvotes). The architecture change was minimal (layer normalization moved to the input of each sublayer, a final layer normalization added after the last block, and the context window extended to 1024 tokens). The finding was that, with enough data and compute, the same architecture and training objective produced markedly more coherent long-form text, and that a sufficiently large zero-shot GPT-2 could perform competitive with fine-tuned baselines on several NLP benchmarks without any task-specific training. That last observation hinted at in-context learning, the subject of a later node in this graph.

What it cannot do by construction

An autoregressive LM has access only to left context at each position. That is exactly right for generation — you cannot condition a generative step on tokens you haven't emitted yet — but it is a handicap for tasks where the answer depends on both directions of context around a target: named-entity recognition, coreference, or reading comprehension where the answer is in the passage to the right of the question. The encoder-only approach of BERT addresses this directly, trading away the ability to generate in exchange for full bidirectional context; the masked-lm node describes that architecture. The contrast between the two regimes is the subject of the encoder-decoder-contrast node.

diagrams.caption: Decoder-only stack: input tokens flow through L causal-masked self-attention blocks, then a linear projection and softmax yield the next-token probability distribution.
diagrams.altText: A top-to-bottom stack. Input tokens (right-shifted) enter an embedding plus positional encoding layer, then pass through L decoder blocks each containing causal self-attention and an FFN. The top block feeds a linear projection to vocab size V, then a row-wise softmax producing the next-token distribution. A dashed annotation shows the right-shifted target: position t predicts token t+1. The cross-entropy loss is noted at the output.
diagrams.prompt: Structural top-to-bottom diagram of a decoder-only autoregressive language model. At the bottom: a box labeled 'x₁ x₂ … xₙ' (input tokens, right-shifted). An upward arrow leads to a box labeled 'embed + pos enc' with shape annotation 'X ∈ ℝⁿ ˣ ᵈmodel'. An upward arrow leads into a large box labeled 'decoder block × L'; inside the block, two inner boxes in sequence: 'causal self-attention (masked — no peeking right)' in red, then 'FFN' in black, connected by a rightward arrow. An ellipsis above the block indicates L blocks total. An upward arrow from the top of the block stack leads to a box labeled 'linear (n × V)' annotated 'projects to vocab logits'. A final upward arrow leads to a box labeled 'softmax → p(xₜ₊₁ | x₁…xₜ)' highlighted in green, with a shape note 'next-token distribution (n × V)'. On the right side, a dashed annotation reading 'target = input shifted left by one: position t predicts token t+1' with a leader arrow pointing toward the block stack. A second dashed annotation at the top reads 'loss: −Σ log p_θ(xₜ | x₁…xₜ₋₁)' pointing at the softmax output. Label every element; structural diagram.

diagrams.caption: The lower-triangular causal mask and the autoregressive feedback loop: each token sees only its own past, and each generated token becomes the next input.
diagrams.altText: Left panel: a 5-by-5 attention score matrix with the upper triangle shaded grey and labeled minus infinity, and the lower triangle plus diagonal shown as dots indicating allowed attention. The diagonal and below are accessible; above-diagonal entries are blocked. Right panel: an autoregressive decoding loop showing a prompt feeding into the model, which outputs a next token, which is appended to the prompt and fed back as input for the next step.

Row axis labeled 'query position (t)'; column axis labeled 'key position (j)'. A caption below reads 'causal mask: position t attends only to j ≤ t'. Right panel: an autoregressive feedback loop. bibliography.annotation: The GPT-1 paper. Introduces the decoder-only pre-training + fine-tuning recipe. See §3 for the architecture (12 layers, 117M params, BooksCorpus) and §3.2 for the training objective and teacher-forcing setup.

bibliography.citation: Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., & Sutskever, I. (2019). "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners." OpenAI technical report.
bibliography.annotation: The GPT-2 paper. Scales the same decoder-only recipe to 1.5B parameters on WebText. §2 describes the architecture modifications (pre-norm, extended context). The zero-shot results that hint at in-context learning are in §3–4.
The clearest visual walkthrough of the decoder-only stack, the causal mask in attention, and the token-generation loop. Highly recommended as the first companion read after the GPT-2 paper's §2.

bibliography.citation: Karpathy, A. "Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code" (nanoGPT / Zero-to-Hero).
bibliography.annotation: Builds a decoder-only GPT in ~200 lines of PyTorch, making the causal mask, the training loop, and the autoregressive generation loop concrete. Ideal for seeing the architecture expressed as running code.
